passage: Devika, you asked why I keep the old group chat but never post. I'm Wasim, and at fifteen I felt invisible at home. Abba worked nights and nobody asked about my day. Then an online community began greeting me by name every morning and saying they were glad I was there. That warmth was real, and I won't pretend it wasn't. I nearly moved my whole life into it. But one night I asked myself: does being welcome make everything they teach true? I couldn't say yes. So I joined the school cricket club, made two friends who could sit beside me, and kept the chat as one small part of my days.

qa.q: How old was Wasim when the online community began greeting Wasim by name?
What was Wasim feeling at home, and why did the community appeal?
qa.a: Wasim felt invisible at home, so a community greeting Wasim by name every morning felt warm and welcome. 🙂

qa.q: What offline step did Wasim take?
qa.a: Wasim joined the school cricket club and made two friends who could sit beside Wasim, keeping the chat as one small part of life.

qa.q: What would probably have been different if Wasim had felt seen at home?
qa.a: The pull of an online welcome would likely have been weaker, since Wasim would not have felt so invisible.

grounding: Wasim feels unseen at home and is warmly welcomed by an online community, finds the warmth real but not proof of truth, and builds offline friendships.
